_about: THE FREEZE (rule 454(a)): every standing line of the 13 counted mouths and two small ones as it was when THE VOICE HOLDS was built. Nothing in a closed mouth changes until he says go for that mouth (records/words_two/the_voice_switch.json). When a mouth is rewritten on his word, these lines are its WAS.

road: what the stranger says: Oye, jefe. Two days no food. I don't want batteries, just something to eat. My brother says ask the ones with guns, they got food.
You fed my little brother. So I tell you straight: three men sit on the next bend with a rifle. I know a way around. And if you want, I walk with you.
The axle, mijo. I got the part, I don't got the arms. One hour of your boys lifting and I owe you. A trucker always pays back, ask anybody.
¡Mira quién es! The arms! I been looking for you. A crate of beans fell off the back of my own truck, if you understand me.
(a delivery drone, face-down, its little speaker looping) Paquete en camino. Package on its way. Paquete en camino. The box under it is sealed with the Network's tape.
Every drone has a camera, amigo. We saw you open our box. You give back eighteen and a little for the trouble, or my friends here come down.
You the one who walked our drone home? Honest people are rare as rain. The Network pays honest. Here.
This road is ours today, my loves. Five batteries a head, or ten for all of you because you dress so ugly I feel sorry. Rick Owens would cry.
My ugly friends who pay! Go, go, free road. And a gift: the men at the overpass are new and scared. Scared men sell cheap.
Fever three days. My wife went for the clinic, she don't come back. If you got water, a little. If you don't, then just tell her I waited.
You're them. He told me. He lived, ¿me oyes? He lived. I got nothing much. I sew. Let me give you something I sewed.
(a courier, two days dead, still holding the strap of a bag. The bag has a Remnants seal. A crow looks at you like you're next in line.)
Darling. The world ended and you still dress like a parking lot. One coat, Balenciaga, real, from the Forum Shops. Twenty batteries and you live forever.
Coyotes, big ones, the lab kind. They follow you since the wash. Gimme three batteries and I show you where they sleep. You kill them, the skins sell.
The dollar was a false god and it died like one. Now everybody worships the battery. Brothers, give one battery to the Church, and the Church remembers your face at the gate.
¡Ayúdame! They say I steal the water, but it's my pump, my father dug it! They're coming. Hide me in your wagon, please.
(a radio taped to a pole, playing a weather report from before. Sunny. Seventy-two. The dollar is up. Then the same report again. Somebody has been changing its batteries.)
You took the batteries out of my radio. My wife recorded that report the morning before. It's the last of her voice. Put four back or I follow you forever.
We quit the Reds. They make us shoot water thieves, kids, everybody. We fight good. Take us, or don't, but don't tell the Reds you saw us.
One hand, high card. You win, I give you twenty. You lose, I take ten. The house always won, mijo. The house is dead now. Let's see.
¡Vengan, vengan! A wedding! Two families stop fighting today. Eat, drink, and if you have a gift, the gift table is the truck bed.
Lab cat. American lion, they said, from a bone in Tule Springs. It took my arm and my partner. It sleeps in the wash. Kill it and the reward is yours, I only want to see it dead.
Good copper in this one, but I need four hands. You help me pull it, we split it. Hour of work. Trades rules, half and half.
Don't be scared. I'm a nurse, I walk at night because the days are too hot. I have bandages and nobody to give them to. Can I walk with you to the next town?
¡Aquí abajo! My foot is stuck in the grate. The water comes when it rains, and it's going to rain. Please.
Inspección. What's in the wagon, jefe? We take a tenth of everything, it's the law now. Our law. Or you can try to argue.
Chato smells water. Four legs, three legs, he smells it better than any machine. Two batteries and he finds you a cistern nobody knows.
(he holds a TV with no back. On it, your own crew, walking this road, from above, ten minutes ago. He smiles.) Everything is recorded. Do you want to see what happens next?
Raiders hit a farm west of here. We're short a gun. Ride with us one hour, the Blues pay what's fair, and we don't forget who stood with us.

Mi patrón's ranch out by Moapa is dust. The cattle went when the feed trucks stopped coming. All I got left is this. A rodeo bullwhip, braided by hand. It cracks louder than a pistol and it don't need bullets. Sixty batteries. In town they want a hundred.

The Golden Cue closed forever, so we make spears out of the cues. Two cues taped long, a knife on the tip. It reaches two houses, jefe, it keeps a dog off you. Twelve batteries. In the market it's seventeen.

Nobody hires me. They see the vest and cross the street. Mira, I'm not crazy. Four cells wired to a switch. If I go down, the switch lets go, and whoever is standing on me goes with me. You want a man nobody wants to get close to? Twelve batteries and I walk with you.

Ey! The {party} delivery to {toward|the next town}, that's us. The axle went. The rest of the convoy is up the road, they don't stop, that's the rule. I got medicine in the back and two guys with bats for a whole valley. Help me push it to the convoy and they pay you, I swear on my mother.
Shh. Get down. That's the {party} convoy coming, to {toward|wherever}. We hit it at the bend. You want a share? Hold the back, nobody gets hurt that matters.
You. The one who warned the {party}. Two of my guys are in their pen now because of you. I'm not here to kill you, I'm here for what they cost me. Twenty.

Count the stones, amigo. One for every car that tried the pass after the dollar went. Fifty-one. The ones that made it don't get a stone. Leave a battery on the pile and you make it down. Everybody who left one made it down. I counted them too.

We're going over to Pahrump. My cousin says there's well water there and nobody counts it. Thirty-two people. The brakes are cooked from the grade and the next part is down. You got a man who knows brakes? We pay what we have.
The pass is ours. Nobody else clears the rockslides, so everybody pays the rock tax. Five. Or pick up a shovel, we got a slide right there, two hours and you walk free.

The {raider} hit the {raided} town last night. They took the water, the cells, my cousin's truck. They're walking home with it right now, you can see their dust. Me, I'm going to my sister. You got a little food for the road?
The {raider} already took the good stuff. They left the doors open. Everybody's in there taking what's left. There's a pharmacy nobody found yet, jefe. You want in?

Listen to this. Somebody tapes cassettes to the fences. Same voice every time, reading the price of eggs. Every week the price is higher. This one says a dozen eggs, one hundred ninety dollars. Dollars, bro. Who is still counting in dollars?
It comes on every night at the same time. BUFFET, NINE NINETY-NINE. Somebody still pays for the cell. My boy watches it for the food. He thinks if he watches long enough they open.

Your crew owes. Not you. One of your men signed for a loan with the Mob before he walked with you. Forty batteries and the interest. A debt doesn't care who you work for now. Pay half today and we write it closed, or we take him.

I ring it for the ones in the houses who died alone after the money went. Nobody came for them, so I come. Every night a different street. Tonight it's this one. Stand with me a minute, hijo, it's only a minute.
Agua del lago! Lake Mead, the deep intake, the third straw. Boiled twice. Three batteries a jug. Food and water is the same thing out here, compa, you know that.
Boss, the battery box is light. Six short. I counted twice. It was me. My sister in Henderson has a boy on an oxygen machine, and the machine eats batteries. I was going to tell you.
Six of the cans from the last town are swelling at the ends. My grandmother said a can that swells will kill you, and she lived through the last time the money went bad.
See that road? I drove it every day, to {place}. Nobody has been in there since the lights went. I know the side door and where they kept the keys. It is about {blocks} blocks from here.
{other} drank the last of the water in the night, boss, my share too. I am going to break {other}'s face unless you tell me why I should not.

A man came through from Pahrump. My mother and my two sisters are still out there. He says the wells went dry on their street and the ranch stopped selling to them. I have to go to them, boss. Or I have to send them something.
Four batteries a pint, paid on the cot. We test you first. The hospitals on the Strip buy everything we take. {man} there looks healthy. Up and walking again by tomorrow.
The bank sold the whole street to a man with a crew, and the crew collects rent in batteries now. Three a week. I paid it for three years. This week I do not have it, so they are taking the door off.
Every house on this street was foreclosed in the first crash, and nobody ever drained the pools. Now they are the only water for a mile. Green, full of mosquitoes. You can have some if you carry it.
There is copper wire in every one of these poles, and copper trades for batteries at the scrap yard. The lights have not been on in years. Help me strip the block and we split it.
Folks! Ninety minutes of your time and breakfast is on us. Real eggs: we keep chickens on the roof now. Vacation ownership is still the smartest money in Nevada. Ask me about week thirty-two.

The casino pays us in its own chips now. Good at its buffet and its store and nowhere else, and the buffet doubled its prices. So we stopped working. Do not cross the line. If you have food, we are on day nineteen.

It still has power. A battery inside it, I think. Every morning I put my card in and it says my balance is zero, and every morning I believe it a little less. Open it if you want. I only want to see it say something else.

We lost the house in the first year of the crash and the car in the second. People say you have walls at {home}. I can cook for twenty and keep a ledger. The kids carry water. We do not need much, only a door that locks.
Pulled it off a foreclosed roof in Summerlin, the bank's notice still taped to the door. A panel lasts thirty years and this one has twenty left in it. I will walk it all the way to {home} myself.

The water district lost its pressure above the second floor everywhere west of Rainbow. A tank on a roof is water for a month. I pulled this one four miles by hand and I cannot pull it one more block.
The library lent seeds before it stopped lending books. Squash, tepary beans, chiles, the ones that take the heat. The rule was you bring back seeds from what you grow. Nobody has brought any back.
I worked for {boss} at {boss_place}. Everybody does, or they leave the valley. I know the way in and where the men sleep. I want food and to be far from here before anybody knows I talked.

The county assessor's maps, every parcel in the valley, printed the week before the servers went dark. I marked where {boss} sits. It is about {boss_blocks} blocks from here. Paper does not need a signal.
This road belongs to {boss} from here to {boss_place}. Everybody pays to use it. Four batteries for the lot of you, or turn around and go the long way.
{boss} is dead and the rest of us have nobody to pay us. I can shoot and I know every room of {boss_place}. Feed me and I will shoot for you instead.
{job_from} sent me about your job: {job}. They need it sooner than you said. If you push, they will remember it. If you do not, they will remember that too.
Heard {job_from} gave you their job: {job}. They gave it to us first, before you came along. Walk away and nobody gets hurt. Or pay us to walk away. Your call.
There are men waiting at the underpass for whoever comes through on business for {job_from}. They have been there since morning. Two batteries and I show you the long way around.
You are working for {job_from}? My daughter lives there. I have not heard from her since the phones went. Take this letter to her. Her name is on it.
We cooked for {boss} for two years at {boss_place}, for nothing, because the door was locked from his side. Now it is open and we do not know where to go. Somebody said you have a place.
You put {boss} down. He was a bad man and he was my brother. I am not here to forgive it. Pay what his life was worth to his mother, or we settle it here.
This is what {boss} took from every stall in {town}, every week, for years. I carried it out of {boss_place} after he fell. It is not mine. It is not yours either. Tell me what to do with it.
{boss_place} is empty since you put {boss} down. People are already fighting over who moves in. Whoever has the sign off the door is the one people listen to. That could be you.
You took our job in {deed_town} and you did not finish it. We gave food up front to the crew we trusted, and we went hungry for it. People there say your name now the way they say a curse.

Nobody came to {deed_town} when you said you would. The men you were paid to stop came instead. My husband is in the ground and my arm will not close. I am not asking you for anything. I wanted you to see it.

The job in {deed_town} went bad. It happens to everybody once. There is a smaller one: the pump on the east side needs a crew to sit on it for four hours tonight. Do it, and we will talk to you again.
There is a song in {deed_town} about the crew that took the job and never came. Everybody knows the words. I can sing it for you. Or you can pay me not to sing it anywhere else.
You did right by {deed_town}. People there will not say it to your face, so I came out to say it. And I brought this: bread from the oven behind the church, and peppers.
I saw what your crew did for {deed_town}. I want to do that. I can shoot, I can carry, and I do not complain. My mother says I am too young. She is wrong.
{deed_town} sent me after you. There are men at the next overpass waiting for whoever comes this way. We owe you, so we are telling you.
Word from {deed_town} is that you keep your word. That is worth something to me. I will sell you food cheap today, or buy yours at a fair price. Most people I would cheat.
road: the answer after his choice: Gracias. I don't forget faces. Neither does my brother.
Five. Okay. That's a can at the post. Gracias, jefe.
Sí. Everybody keeps walking.
Teo. I carry, I watch, I don't complain. Vámonos.
Through the culvert. And there is a dead man's pack down there. Six batteries. Yours.
Your call, jefe. Watch the bend.
Ándale, that's it. I run the Primm road. You'll see me again.
Ten. Pues, fair. Nobody lifts for free no more.
Nobody has time. That's why the trucks stopped.
Six nights for your boys. We're square. Until next time.
Twenty-five, and don't tell my husband.
Paquete... en... (the speaker dies. Eighteen batteries in foam, packed like eggs.)
Gracias por su entrega. Thank you for your delivery. (somebody, somewhere, logged your face.)
Paquete en camino. Paquete en camino.
Smart. The Network forgets fast when it's paid.
They dropped their own batteries running.
They took fifteen and the drone's camera kept rolling.
Twenty. And your name is good on our wire now.
News? The Reds move water on the night of the full moon. And eight batteries, because I like you.
Gracias, gorgeous. Next time you pass, you pass free.
The cart had their whole day's take in it.
They took the ten anyway, and your hat.
Long way is free. Long way is also long.
And five back, because I'm in a mood. Don't get used to it.
Five nights of food for eight. Told you. Scared.
Dios te lo pague. Her name is Lupe. Lupe Ortiz.
You carried a stranger. People there saw you do it.
I'll tell her a group came by. That's something.
A knife, in a sheath I stitched with his old belt. Cut good things with it.
Then I tell everybody in town what you did. That's worth more, maybe.
Fourteen batteries and a letter nobody will get now. The Remnants count their bags.
The crow waits on a sign the whole time. It does not like you.
The crow goes back to work.
The knife. Tragic. But it matches nothing, so it matches everything.
Food! Fashion eats too, my love. Six batteries and my blessing.
Nobody buys today. Everybody dies ugly.
Skins for fifteen batteries at the post, and meat for two nights.
They got into the wagon on the way out.
Okay. They're still following you, though.
Five. Bendito. The sisters will hear your name tonight.
...and on the eighth day the screens went dark and man looked up. Gracias for listening. Nobody listens.
Walk, then. The road listens.
They walk right past. She leaves you three jugs. Three nights of water.
She gives you the jugs anyway. Her father's pump is hers again tonight.
They took her and two of your jugs.
Twelve batteries from the pump men. She doesn't look at you once.
She runs on into the dark.
Four batteries. The report stops on 'the dollar is'. The quiet is worse.
Sunny. Seventy-two. The dollar is up.
Eight. She'll talk for two more weeks. Gracias. Go with God.
He doesn't follow you. But you hear the report in your head all night.
He takes ten and walks back to his pole.
Benny. The other one goes his own way. The Reds will hear, they always hear.
Twenty batteries from a Red patrol. The two boys don't fight it.
Gracias. We were never here.
King. Ay, the king. Take it before I change my mind.
Seven. Bad night for sevens. Gracias.
The lights were on twenty-four hours. Nobody looked up. Now everybody looks up. Go on.
Ten! You eat like family. Take a plate for the road. The whole town will hear.
Eat, eat. Nobody counts at a wedding. Well. My aunt counts.
Next time, then. There's always a next wedding. Or a funeral.
Thirty batteries, my whole savings. He cries like a kid. Gracias.
It's still out there. It knows you now.
It will be. It's always everybody's fight, later.
Half and half, ten each. The Trades will hear you work clean.
¡Rata! I know your faces! The whole Trades will know them!
Pues, more for me.
Thank you. I'll tell the Volunteers who walked me. We look after the ones who look after us.
Bandages, eight batteries' worth at any post. A fair trade at night.
She runs home without saying gracias. Later the whole town knows who did it.
She's out. Scraped up, but out. Gracias, gracias.
It doesn't give. You dig anyway. Forty-five minutes.
Eight batteries and a night of food. Pásale. Have a nice day.
The jefe laughs. 'You got balls. Go.' Nobody pays.
Their cash box. Twenty-five. The cartel will want it back.
They take twenty and the long way of making a point.
Long way around. Smart, maybe.
A cistern under a gas station. Four nights of clean water. Chato wants a scratch.
He likes you. Chato likes everybody. That's his problem.
Static. Then a picture of a cache under a billboard. It's real. Ten batteries.
Static. When you look up he's gone, and so are two nights of food from the wagon.
He turns his head to follow you. Just his head.
Twenty batteries and a handshake. The Blues remember.
The raiders got away. The sergeant doesn't blame you. Much.
Busy. Everybody's busy until it's their farm.
Take care of it. It took my abuelo a whole winter.
Food. Okay. Food I can't braid. It's yours.
Sí. Nobody needs a cowboy in a city with no cows.
Hold it at the back, not the middle. The middle is for the felt.
Four for the tape and the blade. Your tape job is ugly, but it holds.
Okay. The dogs don't care how cool you look.
Bueno. Walk in front of me, not behind. Everybody learns that the first day.
Home. Sí. I'll eat first and think about home after.
Like everybody. It's okay. I'm used to the street.
Eighteen, from the convoy boss. He didn't say thank you. He never does.
Antibiotics and a box of crackers. The {party} will hear about this.
Two guys with bats. You were wrong about them.
Sí. The convoy left us too.
Your share is thirty-four. Ruiz counts it twice, slow, so you can see.
The guards were ready. Ruiz ran first.
The convoy boss pays twelve for the warning. Ruiz saw your face.
Smart. You never saw me.
Twenty. Now we're nothing to each other. That's the best thing I can be.
He had ten on him and a photo of a dog.
He took twelve and your hat.
Ja. With the {party}. Okay, jefe. You're funny. I'll be around.
Bueno. Keep left at the burned bus. Right goes to the drop.
Nothing happens. The wind comes up the pass and the stone man doesn't look at you again.
Two coyotes, thin as wire. The stone man adds two stones.
You drop the batteries running. The pile gets them back.
Fifty-one. I'll leave room for one more.
Twelve batteries and two bags of tortillas. Thirty-two people wave at you out the back window.
Fourteen. They needed brakes more than food, but okay.
Okay. We'll go slow. Pray for the slow.
Five. Mutual aid, compa. The rocks don't care who's in charge.
You dig. They pay you four for the extra rocks. Nobody owns this pass and everybody works it.
Fifteen in their tax box. The slide is still there.
They take ten and your shovel would have been cheaper.
Que Dios te lo pague. Everybody from the {raided} town remembers the ones who gave.
Twenty-eight batteries off their backs, and the truck. Lupe's cousin comes for it on foot.
There were more of them than dust. You got out.
Sí. Everybody's walking today.
Fourteen in cells and two cans. A woman in a doorway watches you carry it out.
Put it back for who? For the {raider}? They'll be back next week for the TV.
Okay. More for me.
After the eggs, milk. After the milk, ten seconds of a crowd breathing. Then the date, and it is next week.
Two. Keep it. I don't want it in my house anymore.
Yeah. Don't listen. That's what I should've done.
He eats it looking at the sign. He says it tastes like nine ninety-nine.
Six in the cell. The sign goes dark. The boy doesn't cry. He just keeps looking at it.
It's okay. It comes on again tomorrow.
Closed. Clean. I'll write your name in the good column.
Sensible. He'll work it off. They always do, eventually.
We always do. It's sixty next time. The ledger doesn't sleep.
Thirty-one doors. He says each number out loud. Nobody opens one.
One candle a house. That's tonight's street. Gracias.
Go with God. Somebody will ring for you too.
Two jugs. Drink the old one first, the new one keeps.
Lower every year. The first straw sucks air since 2022, the second since 2027. The third is the last one. After that we drink the river, and the river is Arizona's.
Okay. The sun will sell it to you later, more expensive.
{man} sends them south with the next cart. No thank you. None needed.
{man} pays it back over a week and never says another word about it.
In the morning {man}'s bedroll is gone, and six more batteries with it.
{man} goes with nothing but the clothes on. Four of the six are still in the bedroll.
Three nights of food into a ditch. Nobody gets sick.
Boiled long and eaten fast. Boiling kills the poison, the cook says. Nobody gets sick, and the food is kept.
{man} is sick all night: the cramps, then the double vision. {man} will be weak for days.
They taste like tin. Nobody gets sick, this time.
By morning {man} cannot stand up straight. It will be days before {man} can fight.
{man} draws it in the dirt for everybody: the side door, the loading dock, the bend in the road. {place} is on your map now.
{man} looks down the road a while longer, then picks up the pack.
Everybody drinks. Nobody fights. The cans stay full another day.
It is over in a minute. {other} has a split lip and a rib that hurts to breathe on for a few days.
{man} shakes every hand in the company and walks west at first light.
Five batteries go west with a cart driver {man} trusts. {man} stays.
{man} stays, and does not sleep much.
In the morning {man}'s bedroll is gone, and five batteries with it.
An hour on a cot. {man} comes back pale and four batteries heavier, and will be slow for a day.
The man in the van shrugs. There is a line behind you.
The crew counts the three twice and puts the door back on. The street saw you do it.
Their week's take, six batteries, and the door stays on.
They took her rent out of your pocket instead.
The door comes off behind you.
Two hours over a fire made of a fence. It tastes like the bottom of a pool. It is water.
Nobody gets sick. This time.
{man} is burning up by night. The mosquitoes, or the water.
Three hours of wire, four batteries at the scrap yard. The street is darker than it was, and the people on it know who did it.
He climbs down and spits. Somebody on the corner nods at you.
Ninety minutes that take two hours. The eggs are real. He shakes every hand twice.
He hands you the deed to week thirty-two of room 1411. The room has no wall on one side. He calls it the view.
He calls after you that the offer ends today. It has ended today for eleven years.
They pass it down the line. Somebody writes your company's name on a sign.
The casino's store pays well for what you carry. On the way out, nobody on the line looks at you.
Day nineteen. She turns back to the line.
Inside: forty thousand in twenties and the machine's own battery, still good. You take the battery. The screen goes dark in the middle of a word.
Behind you the machine asks her if she would like a receipt.
Two nights of food for the walk, and a door at {home}. She asks where the ledger is before she asks where she sleeps.
She counts the food twice and thanks you once. The kids are already walking.
He pushes the cart toward {home} without being asked twice. The bank's notice is still stuck to the back of the panel.
Food, not batteries: he eats the first can before he lets go of the cart.
Six batteries and a handshake. He shows you how to bleed the air out of the line before he goes.
Three hours of pulling. He sells the water by the bucket at {town} and pays you three batteries out of the first bucket.
Three batteries for the library, she says, and writes your name on the card in pencil. Due back next year.
Two hours with a drawer under each arm. At {town} she sets the catalogue on a table and opens for business.
He draws it in the dirt with a stick: the gate, the yard, the room where {boss} sleeps. Then he is gone up the wash.
Five batteries buys a seat on a cart to Barstow. He tells you everything about {boss_place} on the way to the cart.
Four batteries. Nobody in {town} will look at you the same way, and the man does not look at you at all.
Parcel numbers, lot lines, and a red circle around {boss_place} in ballpoint.
Two hours hauling his rolls of paper to {town}. He pays with the map that has the red circle on it.
They roll one cart out of the way and roll it back behind you.
Two and a half hours around through the washes. Their fire is still burning when you look back.
The carts go into the ditch and the tolls in their can go into your wagon.
They take the toll anyway, and more for the trouble.
Three nights of food up front. He hands you the rifle to hold while he eats, and asks for it back after.
Six batteries. By morning eleven men are walking north on the 95 with their rifles slung, and the street is quiet.
Extra rations to keep the men on their feet. The runner goes back to {job_from} with the word that you are coming.
The runner writes it down word for word. {job_from} will read it out loud, he says.
Four batteries in his saddlebag. The motorbike goes the other way, and so does his crew.
They leave the motorbike's battery behind. {job_from} hears who kept their job.
They take four batteries and laugh about it. The job is still yours, if you can still do it.
Two hours of back yards and broken fences. You never see the underpass.
Nobody at the underpass but a burned-out car. The kid was lying, or they got bored.
A shot from the dark at the far end. {man} is hit in the arm before you are through.
Half an hour while he writes one more line at the bottom. {job_from} will know who brought it.
He puts the letter back in his coat and keeps waiting for the bus.
Three nights of food for the walk. They go toward your place singing something from before.
They split it six ways and thank you six times. By tonight {town} knows who opened the door.
He counts them twice and walks away without a word. The road is quiet after.
It is over. His rifle had two batteries taped to the stock.
He takes the six batteries anyway, and leaves you lying in the road.
An hour and a half, stall by stall, back to who it came from. Nobody in {town} will forget it.
Six batteries in the box. The man walks off. In {town} they say you took over where {boss} stopped.
Two hours with a crowbar. The sign goes on the cart to your place, and the squatters stop arguing.
An hour to get it burning. The smoke from {boss_place} shows from {town}, and people come out to watch it go.
He takes them to {deed_town}. It does not make it right, he says, but it is something they will remember.
He spits on the road and walks back toward {deed_town}.
She takes it without looking at you. It is the only thing you can do here.
She watches you go. Someone from {deed_town} is watching too.
Four quiet hours on the pump. Three batteries and a nod from the elder. {deed_town} will talk to you again.
The elder turns the mule around without a word.
He pockets the batteries and starts another song, about something else.
He sings it all the way through. It is a good song. {town} will be singing it by tonight.
Four nights of bread and peppers. She waves the whole way back to {deed_town}.
She looks at you a long time and nods. {deed_town} will hear that too.

Eleven years I dealt blackjack. I been in this line every morning since the dollar went. Nobody is behind the window. The screen says NOW SERVING 211 and I am 211, so. You hiring, jefe? I count fast and I don't flinch.

Two tours, then fourteen years security on a casino floor. I know how to stand in one place, I been practicing in this line. Give me something that shoots, hermano, and a place to stand.
Line cook. I can make dinner out of nothing, and nothing is what everybody has now, verdad? I'll cook for the whole crew for one bowl of it.
I drove a cab on the Strip, then a truck out to Primm. Every road in this valley, I know which ones are still roads, te lo juro. The screen in there flickers at night. Still 211.
{yes}
Nobody pushes. They have been in line too long to push. Somebody at the back starts clapping, then stops.

Everything with a plug went the first week, jefe. The generators, the propane, the chainsaws, the batteries off the end caps. Then the plywood for the windows, then the wire. What's left is paint and doorknobs. A crew sleeps in the lumber aisle now. Listen. The music. The back-up battery still plays it, the same eleven seconds, all night.
Behind the returns desk: a crowbar still on its card and three lantern batteries in a return nobody ever processed.
One battery, out of a smoke detector. Everybody forgets the smoke detectors.
They had the last framing hammer in the store and two batteries. The manager folds their blankets and puts them out on the curb.
They know the aisles better than you. The music kept playing the whole time.

Thirty years I cut keys here. Nobody needs a key now, everything is open. Mira, all open. The west side went slower than the east. There's still some in receiving, if you know where the dock door is. I know where it is.
A pallet nobody unwrapped. A pipe wrench and three batteries in the shrink wrap. He cuts you a key for the dock door. Habit.
Somebody found the dock first. One battery in a forklift's dash.

The gas stopped coming down the pipe the year the dollar went, jefe. Nineteen units, and one still turns: they cut a hatch in the old 1954 boiler and feed it pallets and tires. That one unit charges every battery on this side of the valley. Whoever holds this plant prints the money. Listen. The control room still calls out the load every hour. Nobody here is reading it.
Three nights of food for the crew, and two hours on the bus bar. Six batteries come off the rack warm. The load call says the same number it always says.
Their charging racks, twelve batteries full. The operator keeps feeding the boiler. Somebody always holds the mint, he says; today it was you.
They held. Six of yours went on their rack before you got out the gate.

Three turbines and not one cubic foot of gas, hermano. The pipe is dry since the dollar. Once a week I turn the shafts by hand so the bearings don't seize, because the day the gas comes back, whoever has a turbine that turns owns the whole valley. The stacks still have their lights. Red, every night, for airplanes that don't come.
The plant kept a whole room of batteries to start the turbines with no grid. Ten still hold. The watcher says that was the only way to ever start them again.
Most of the room was dead, the acid gone to crust. Four still hold.
Six batteries in their truck and the pick they were pulling copper with. The watcher counts the breakers they left. Most of them.
They kept the switchyard. The copper goes out on their truck to somebody who pays.

Nobody fed the big tank since the power went, jefe. Fifteen kinds of shark, the rays, the sawfish. Now there are four sharks and they are very big. The tunnel under the tank still holds. Some nights the emergency lights come on by themselves and you can see them going round and round over your head. The glass is not my problem. The glass is what holds.
The gift shop on the far side: flashlights still boxed, four good batteries, and a shelf of candy. Over your head, the whole way, something kept pace.
Somebody cleared the gift shop first. One battery in a toy shark. Over your head, the whole way, something kept pace.
Two rays and a grouper off the top of the big tank, four nights of food. The sharks watched the line the whole time.
Something took the net and whatever you were holding it with. One small fish from the touch pool.

When the staff stopped coming I opened every kennel, so they would have a chance. Most of them went to the washes, those are your wild dogs now. Some came back. These ones never left, and I feed them what I find. Mira, the brindle one. He picks people. Tonight he is sitting by your boots. The intake bell still rings at nine every morning. There is nobody at the door.
Okay. The brindle comes, and I come with the brindle. The others know where the food is now. Two nights of food for the road, sí.
The dogs eat in a row, oldest first. People on Mojave Road hear a crew fed the shelter dogs.

Welcome to the museum, my friend. The family keeps it now. It's ours, it was always ours. The chair is downstairs, the wall from Chicago with the bullet holes. The tour is free. What you do after the tour, that has a price. Ask me about the Kefauver room. Everybody who testified in there is dead now, every single one, so the room is very quiet, sabes.
The chair, the wall, the hearing room. At the end the docent writes your company's name in a ledger. He says it is the guest book.
Ten batteries, counted twice on the courthouse steps. The family remembers who collects.
They did not pay, and now the family has two debts to collect.

The lab people came here first, before the fossil beds. They took samples from everything: the mammoth tooth, the sloth hair in the case, the camel. They did not take the T. rex. You can't, mano, the DNA is gone after a million years. That's chemistry, not money. So he is the one thing in this valley that is never coming back. Some nights his motor still roars on the backup battery.

Here is the rule they worked by. Ice Age and after, a million years at the most, from frozen ground and dry caves. A living animal the right size to carry the baby. The wolf had a dog, the mammoth an elephant. The T. rex has nothing. Anybody who tells you they saw a dinosaur is lying to you.
Five batteries out of the T. rex's backup bank. The keeper does not watch. That night, for the first time, the roaring stops.

We're still on the air, jefe. Thursdays, if the generator starts. Nobody has a TV, so we put the picture on the mast, the lights, and people read it from across the valley. Mostly we read the names of who is missing. Sometimes the camera in studio B comes on by itself and there is somebody at the desk we don't know.
One minute on the mast, Thursday: your company's name and that you take work. People three towns over read it in the lights.
The camera's battery packs, four of them, charged. Nobody at the desk. The red light on the camera stays on after you take its battery.
One pack. The chair at the anchor desk was warm.

Two hundred and fifty buses, jefe, and not one drop of diesel. The mechanics stayed because the roof holds and the wash bay still gives water. Every faction wants a bus: a bus is a wagon for twenty men. The new ones were electric, mira, and their battery banks are still in them. Every one of the signs up front still says NOT IN SERVICE. Somebody keeps washing them.
Four hours under an electric bus with the yard boss's wrench. Six cells still hold a charge. The bus sits a little higher on its springs when you are done.
Nineteen years on the RTC's buses. Three nights of food and I go where the wagon goes, sí. I can keep anything with wheels rolling.

Lettuce, kale, basil, in towers, under a roof, on a cup of water a plant. That was the whole idea, before. Now it is the only food in the valley that grows under a roof, hermano, and it grows only while the fans and the pumps run. Every battery you bring me is a week of greens. At night the purple lights show from the freeway, and people come.
A crate of greens, cut this morning: four nights for the company. Three batteries go straight onto the pump's rack.
They broke on the doors and ran. The grower fills your wagon with greens and turns the purple lights down.
They were through the plastic before you were up. Two towers are gone, and two nights of your own food.

The county opened this gym as a cooling station every summer: water, chairs, the air conditioning. Now it is the only cold room for a mile, on a generator that runs on whatever anybody brings it. Mira, in August people sleep here in rows, and the old ones do not wake up if the power goes. Every battery is a night of cold air for forty people.
Five batteries on the generator's rack. Forty people sleep cold tonight, and the street knows whose batteries they are.
Two nights of food and she comes. She has kept men alive in the heat for six summers, she says, and she counts your water before your batteries.

Five acres of rides under a pink glass roof, mano. The glass still keeps the sun off, that is why people live in here. The coaster has its own battery room so a run could finish in a blackout. Every night at eleven it runs once, empty, and nobody here starts it. A crew took the arcade and they charge us to walk past it.
Four hours in the battery room under the lift hill. Eight cells still hold. At eleven the coaster does not run.
Three cells. The rest are swollen and hot to the touch. At eleven the coaster runs anyway.
The crew runs out past the carousel. The people under the dome walk past the arcade for free again.
They charge you for the trouble, and for walking past.

Forty head left, jefe, out of four hundred. The springs still run, that is the only reason we are alive. Everybody in the valley wants beef and nobody wants to herd. The rustlers come down from Blue Diamond on the full moon. Mira, the old ranch house, the Hughes house. The phone in there still rings sometimes. The line has been cut since before I came.
A side of beef, salted, six nights for the company. Six batteries in the foreman's coffee can. One a night, he says, same as the stall.
The rustlers ran for the hills without the herd. The foreman pays in beef and batteries and tells the ranches up the road.
They took six head and two nights of your food off the wagon. The foreman counts the herd again.

Forty motorhomes and not one with gas, hermano. Nobody here is going anywhere, so we fish. The lake went down a hundred feet, the marina sits on the mud like a dead boat. Every winter the roaming people come in off the roads and stay till spring. Oye, the camp host's sign still says THREE NIGHT LIMIT. Some of us have been here eleven years.
Five nights of striped bass, dried on a line between two motorhomes. Fish is cheaper than beef out here. Everybody has a rod.
Eleven years on site 31. I know every road to every water there is. Two nights of food and I'm yours, sí.
map: your second: Oye. Posts on the phone are work. Touch one, it lights up.
Crew on the road. One touch sizes them up, a second goes.
Town ahead. Inside: work on the board, and men for hire.
That's the work, mano: fight, get paid. Batteries feed us.
{name} heals in camp. A dead man doesn't. Cuidado.
New blood eats too. {per} batteries a night, every man.
Every night the crew eats. No batteries, a man walks.
{pay} batteries, for what got here. Gracias.
They got me. {days} days, then I'm back.
{name} didn't get up, carnal. He's gone.
